interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the heat in the switch climb from 40 W to a 3000 W peak when you drag the gate from fully on to half on, where 300 V meets 10 A at once.
interactive.title: The switch and its heat
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
A short lesson in fourteen small screens. Most show one picture, the switch and its heat. A 600 V DC supply feeds a 30 Ω load through a power transistor, the switch. Both values are chosen for the example. A picker chooses BJT, MOSFET or IGBT, and its buttons wrap onto two lines on a narrow phone. The symbol and the control lead's name, base or gate, follow the pick. A gate slider runs from 0% to 100% in steps of 5%. Screen 1 shows only the slider. A small arrow on the control lead shows its current. A BJT takes a steady current into its base while on. A MOSFET's or an IGBT's gate takes a brief pulse only while the setting changes, in as it rises and out as it falls.

Between off and on, the switch acts like a resistor in series with the load. At a setting s, as a fraction, it takes 600 × (1 − s) volts, but never less than its 2 V drop, a value chosen for the example. The current is (600 − the switch's voltage) ÷ 30. The heat in the switch is its voltage times its current. Three readouts show these, wrapping onto two lines on a narrow phone, and a heat bar fills with the heat. From screen 3, a plot shows the heat against the gate setting. It is a hump: zero off, 3000 W at half on and 40 W fully on. The peak is V² ÷ (4R), here 600² ÷ 120 = 3000 W.

From screen 5, a junction thermometer stands by the bar. The junction is the silicon inside. A heat sink of 0.5 °C per watt carries the heat to air at 40 °C, both chosen for the example. So the junction reads 40 + 0.5 × the heat. A line marks a rating of 150 °C, chosen too. Above it the thermometer turns red, and past 200 °C it runs off the top.

In switching mode, the switch flips fully on and off, on half the time. A frequency slider runs from 1 to 20 kHz in steps of 1 kHz. A strip shows a few cycles of the switch's voltage and current, slowed down. Each edge is a straight sweep through the hump, taking 0.5 µs, chosen for the example. A red flash marks each edge, drawn far wider than 0.5 µs so it shows, as a note on the strip says. The heat readout shows the average: half of 40 W while on, plus 2 mJ a cycle times the frequency. The heat bar splits into its on part and its edges part.

A load switch picks Resistor or Coil. The coil has the same 30 Ω and 10 mH, chosen for the example. A tick box adds a freewheeling diode across it. An Open button turns the switch off while the coil carries 19.9 A. With no diode, the switch's voltage jumps in a red spike off the top of its 1000 V scale. With the diode, it steps to 600 V plus the diode's 0.7 V, about 601 V. The coil's current then dies away round the diode, with a time constant of L ÷ R = 10 mH ÷ 30 Ω, about 0.33 ms.

The screens.

1, show: The switch. IGBT, steady, resistor, gate at 100%. Only the gate slider shows. The words: “A transistor is a switch you work with a small signal on a third lead. Its heat is the voltage across it times the current through it. Here it feeds a 30 Ω load from 600 V DC. That is close to a 440 V drive's DC link. Fully off, the whole 600 V sits across it, but almost no current flows. Fully on, about 20 A flows with only 2 V across it. That makes 2 × 20 = 40 W.” Read: fully on, the readouts show 2 V across the switch, a current of 19.9 A and 40 W of heat. Still: IGBT, steady, resistor, gate 100%.

2, a puzzle: the gate stands at 0%, and the readouts are hidden. “The gate is off, and 600 V sits across the switch. How much heat does it make?” Offered: “Almost none, as almost no current flows”; “The most of any setting, from the full 600 V”; “About 40 W, the same as fully on”. Hint for the most: “Heat is volts times amps. How many amps flow when it is off?” Hint for 40 W: “Fully on, 2 V meets 20 A. What current meets the 600 V when it is off?” Why: “Almost none. Heat is the voltage times the current. Off, only a tiny leakage current flows. So 600 V times almost nothing is almost nothing. The picture draws that leakage as zero.” A right Check shows the readouts: 600 V, 0.0 A and 0 W.

3, show: Half on. Steady, resistor, the gate from 100% to 50%. The words: “Between off and on, the transistor acts like a resistor in series with the load. Drag the gate to half on, 50%. The switch now takes half the supply, 300 V. Half the current flows, 10 A. Both are large at once. So the switch makes 300 × 10 = 3000 W. The plot shows the heat against the gate setting. It is a hump. At each end, the voltage or the current is near zero. In the middle, neither is.” Read: at half on, the readouts show 300 V, 10.0 A and 3000 W. The plot's dot sits on top of the hump. Still: gate 50%.

4, a puzzle: the gate at 100%, the plot hidden. “Which gate setting makes the switch hottest?” Offered: “Half on”; “Fully on, with the most current”; “Fully off, with the most voltage”. Hint for fully on: “Fully on, how much voltage is across the switch?” Hint for fully off: “Fully off, how much current flows?” Why: “Half on. There 300 V meets 10 A, which is 3000 W. Fully on, 20 A meets only 2 V. Fully off, 600 V meets almost no current. So half on is no safe middle. It is the hottest place to leave this switch. Held part on on purpose, with small signals, a transistor is an amplifier. That different job is taught in Instrumentation and control.” A right Check draws the plot with its hump.

5, show: Heat into temperature. The thermometer appears, the gate at 100% and then 50%. The words: “The heat has to leave through a heat sink. Its thermal resistance says how far the junction, the silicon inside, rises above the air for each watt. Say 0.5 °C per watt, with the air at 40 °C. Fully on, 40 W lifts the junction 40 × 0.5 = 20 °C, to 60 °C. Half on, 3000 W would lift it 1500 °C. Say this transistor is rated to 150 °C. It fails long before that.” Read: fully on, the thermometer reads 60 °C. At half on, it runs off the top in red. Still: gate 50%.

6, a puzzle: the gate at 100%, the thermometer at 60 °C. “The junction may reach 150 °C. The air is at 40 °C. Each watt lifts the junction 0.5 °C. How much heat can this heat sink shed?” Offered: “About 220 W”; “About 300 W”; “About 55 W”. Hint for 300 W: “Count the rise from the air at 40 °C, not from zero.” Hint for 55 W: “Each watt adds 0.5 °C. So divide the rise by 0.5. Don't multiply.” Why: “About 220 W. The junction may rise 150 − 40 = 110 °C. Each watt lifts it 0.5 °C. So 110 ÷ 0.5 = 220 W. Fully on, 40 W is well inside that. Half on, 3000 W is more than thirteen times too much.” A right Check marks 220 W on the heat bar.

7, show: Three devices, one job. The gate at 50%, the picker from BJT to MOSFET to IGBT. The words: “Three kinds of power transistor do this job. A BJT needs a steady current into its base to stay on. A big one may need 5 A there to pass 100 A. That is a heavy load for its control circuit. A MOSFET turns on with a voltage on its gate. Its gate draws almost no current except while it changes over. An IGBT puts a MOSFET's gate in charge of a bipolar output. It handles high voltages and currents, but turns off more slowly. Pick each one at half on. The heat stays at 3000 W.” Read: at half on, the heat reads 3000 W with each device picked. Only the symbol, the name of its control lead and the base current arrow change. Still: IGBT, gate 50%.

8, a puzzle: the IGBT at half on. “You swap the IGBT for a MOSFET and leave it half on. What happens to the heat?” Offered: “It stays at about 3000 W”; “It falls a long way, as the gate takes no steady current”; “It falls to nothing, as a MOSFET is a better switch”. Hint for falls a long way: “The gate's current is tiny either way. Which voltage and current make the heat?” Hint for nothing: “Half on, any of these switches takes 300 V and passes 10 A here.” Why: “It stays at about 3000 W. Half on, the switch still takes 300 V and passes 10 A. That is 300 × 10 = 3000 W, whatever the device. The gate drive changes what the control circuit must supply. It does not change the heat in the switch's main path.” A right Check picks MOSFET, and the heat reads 3000 W.

9, show: The edges. Switching mode at 10 kHz, the gate slider hidden. The words: “Flipping it fully on and off makes far less heat. On half the time, the load still averages about 300 V. But each edge takes time, say 0.5 µs, sweeping through the hump. A straight sweep averages a sixth of 600 V × 20 A, which is 2000 W. So each edge costs 2000 W × 0.5 µs = 1 mJ. This switching loss is the energy per switching times the frequency.[^1] At 10 kHz, two edges a cycle make 20 W. The on half adds 20 W, so 40 W in all.” Read: in switching mode at 10 kHz, the heat bar splits into 20 W on and 20 W in the edges. The heat reads 40 W, and the thermometer 60 °C. Still: switching, 10 kHz.

10, a puzzle: switching mode at 10 kHz, the edges making 20 W. “You raise the frequency to 20 kHz. What do the edges make now?” Offered: “About 40 W”; “About 20 W, as each edge costs the same”; “About 10 W, as each cycle is shorter”. Hint for 20 W: “Each edge costs the same. How many edges come each second now?” Hint for 10 W: “A shorter cycle means more edges each second, not fewer.” Why: “About 40 W. Each cycle costs about 2 mJ, 1 mJ an edge. At 20,000 cycles a second, that is 2 mJ × 20,000 = 40 W. The on part stays at 20 W. So the switch makes 60 W in all. The junction reaches 70 °C.” A right Check sets 20 kHz, and the heat reads 60 W.

11, show: The coil kicks back. Coil, steady, fully on. The switch opens with no diode. Then the diode is ticked, and it opens again. The words: “A coil keeps its current going, as v = L di/dt says. Contactors and motor windings are coils. Open the switch with no diode, and the coil's current has nowhere to go. The switch tries to stop it in about 0.5 µs. So di/dt is huge, and the switch takes a spike far above the supply. A freewheeling diode across the coil gives it a path round. It points so the supply cannot push current through it. Tick the diode and open it again. Now the coil sees only the diode's drop, about 0.7 V.[^2]” Read: with no diode, opening the switch sends its voltage up in a red spike off the top of the scale. With the diode ticked, opening it again steps the switch's voltage to about 601 V. The coil's current then dies away round the diode. Still: coil, diode ticked, after Open.

12, a puzzle: the coil, no diode, fully on. “The switch opens on the coil with no diode. What voltage does the switch see?” Offered: “A spike far above 600 V”; “600 V, the supply”; “Zero, as the current stops”. Hint for 600 V: “The coil's current can't stop at once on its own. What does v = L di/dt give for a sudden stop?” Hint for zero: “A sudden stop in a coil's current is what makes its voltage jump.” Why: “A spike far above 600 V. The switch tries to force the coil's current from 19.9 A to zero in about 0.5 µs. So di/dt is huge, and so is L di/dt. That voltage adds to the supply across the switch. It can break the switch down. With the diode, the switch sees only about 601 V.” A right Check presses Open, and the red spike runs off the top.

13, a mixed puzzle: steady, resistor, IGBT. “You want the load to average 300 V from the 600 V supply. Which way keeps the IGBT coolest?” Offered: “Flip it fully on and off, on half the time”; “Hold the gate at half on”; “Either way, as the load gets 300 V both ways”. Hint for half on: “Half on, the IGBT takes 300 V and passes 10 A. What heat is that?” Hint for either way: “The load's average is the same. Compare the heat in the switch.” Why: “Flip it. At 10 kHz, it makes about 40 W: 20 W on and 20 W in its edges. Held half on, it makes 3000 W. The load averages about 300 V both ways. But the switch's heat differs by about 75 times.” A right Check sets switching mode at 10 kHz, and the heat reads 40 W.

14, a mixed puzzle: steady, resistor, the gate at 90%, the readouts hidden. “The gate stands at 90%, nearly on. Can the 220 W heat sink cope?” Offered: “No, the switch makes about 1080 W”; “Yes, nearly on is close to the 40 W of fully on”; “No, it makes the 3000 W of half on”. Hint for yes: “At 90%, the switch still takes a tenth of 600 V. What current meets it?” Hint for 3000 W: “At 90%, the voltage is lower than at half on. Work out V × I.” Why: “No. At 90%, the switch takes 60 V and passes 18 A. That is 60 × 18 = 1080 W. It is about five times what the heat sink can shed. Fully on, its voltage falls to about 2 V and the heat to 40 W.” A right Check shows the readouts: 60 V, 18.0 A and 1080 W, and the thermometer runs off the top.

Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Each puzzle offers three answers, stacked so each wraps onto more lines on a narrow phone. A wrong pick gets its one-line hint. Why? explains, and Continue moves on.
interactive.ignores: The picture gives all three devices the same 2 V drop fully on. Real ones differ. A MOSFET's drop grows with its current. Off, the leakage current is drawn as zero. Real leakage is tiny but not nil. The thermometer settles at once. A real heat sink takes time to warm up. Its one thermal resistance stands for a chain, from junction to case, case to sink and sink to air. Each edge is drawn as a straight sweep through a resistive load's hump. With a coil load, a real edge holds nearly the full current while the voltage swings. So it costs more. The power the gate drive uses is left out. The switching strip is slowed down. A cycle at 10 kHz lasts only 0.1 ms.

explain.text:
A power transistor is a switch you work with a small signal on its control lead. In a converter, it is kept fully on or fully off. That way it controls the load while making little heat. Held half on, it would turn far more of the power into heat.

The heat in any switch is the voltage across it times the current through it. Take 600 V DC feeding a 30 Ω load. That is close to a 440 V drive's DC link. Fully off, the whole 600 V sits across the switch. Only a tiny leakage current flows. So the heat is tiny. Fully on, about 20 A flows. A real transistor still keeps a small drop, say 2 V. So it makes about 2 × 20 = 40 W.

Half on, it acts like a resistor in series with the load. It takes half the supply, 300 V, and passes half the current, 10 A. Now both are large at once. So it makes 300 × 10 = 3000 W. The heat peaks at half on, because at each end one of them is near zero. For a resistive load, that peak is V² ÷ (4R), where V is the supply and R the load. Here that is 600² ÷ 120 = 3000 W. A transistor held part on on purpose, with small signals, is an amplifier. That different job is taught in Instrumentation and control.

Heat becomes temperature through the heat sink. Its [[thermal resistance]] says how far the junction, the silicon inside, rises above the air for each watt. Say 0.5 °C per watt, with the air at 40 °C. Fully on, 40 W lifts the junction 20 °C, to 60 °C. Half on, 3000 W would lift it 1500 °C. Say the transistor is rated to 150 °C. It fails long before that. This is why an IGBT should not be run half on.

Switching has its own cost. No switch changes over instantly. During each edge, it sweeps through half on. So each edge makes a burst of heat. This [[switching loss]] is the energy per switching times the switching frequency.[^1] Say each edge takes 0.5 µs. A straight sweep through the hump averages a sixth of 600 V × 20 A, which is 2000 W. So each edge costs 2000 W × 0.5 µs = 1 mJ, or 2 mJ a cycle. At 10 kHz, the edges make 20 W. At 20 kHz, they make 40 W. On half the time, the on-state heat averages 20 W. So switching makes about 40 W at 10 kHz. Held half on, it makes 3000 W. Both give the load about 300 V on average.

Three kinds of power transistor share the job. A BJT, a bipolar transistor, turns on with a current into its base. That current must flow all the time it is on. For a big one, that is a burden. To pass 100 A, it may need 5 A of base current.[^3] A MOSFET turns on with a voltage on its gate. Its gate draws almost no current except while it changes over. An IGBT puts a MOSFET's gate in charge of a bipolar output. It suits high voltages and currents. Its cost is a slower turn-off than a BJT. The heat rule is the same for all three.

Coils add a danger of their own. A coil keeps its current going, as v = L di/dt says. Open its switch, and the current has no other path. The switch tries to stop it in about 0.5 µs, the edge time. So di/dt is huge. The coil can throw a spike across the switch, far above the supply. A [[freewheeling diode]] across the coil gives the current a path round. It points so the supply cannot push current through it. The current flows on through the diode. So the coil sees only the diode's drop, about 0.7 V.[^2] The switch then sees the supply plus that drop, about 601 V. This picture is simplified. It uses one fixed on drop and straight edges. Real devices differ in both. Coil loads also make each edge cost more. **A power transistor in a converter is kept fully on or fully off. Half on, its voltage times its current makes far more heat.**

analogy.text: A transistor held half on works like a series resistance that cuts a load's power. An old resistance starter is one. It controls the current by burning the difference as heat. A series resistance equal to the load takes half the supply at half the full current. That is the same 3000 W peak. A transistor kept fully on or fully off works like a contactor. Closed, it drops almost nothing. Open, it passes nothing. Either way, it stays cool.
analogy.breaks: A contactor switches now and then. Its contacts drop almost nothing. A transistor in a drive switches thousands of times a second. It keeps a volt or two when fully on. So its edges and its on-state drop both make heat. A contactor's make far less.

practice.text:
An off transistor is not isolation. A little current still leaks through it. Its control circuit can also turn it back on. Isolate and prove dead, as for any other circuit.

- To find a switch's heat, find the voltage across it and the current through it in each state.
- Fully on, the heat is its on-state drop times the load current.
- Fully off, it is the supply times a tiny leakage current, close to nothing.
- Half on is the worst case. With a resistive load, it peaks at V² ÷ (4R), where V is the supply and R the load.
- Add the switching loss, the energy per switching times the frequency.
- The junction's rise is the total heat times the thermal resistance in °C per watt.
- Add the air temperature and compare the result with the device's rating.
- Fit a freewheeling diode across a DC coil that a transistor switches. Point it so the supply cannot push current through it. Many devices already carry one, so check before adding another.

**Rule of thumb:** in a converter, keep a power transistor fully on or fully off. Its heat lives in the half-on middle and in every pass through it.

**Worked example:** an IGBT switches 400 V DC into a 10 Ω load. Say it drops 2 V fully on. It passes about 40 A. So it makes about 2 × 40 = 80 W while on. On half the time, that averages 40 W. Say each cycle costs 3 mJ, and it switches at 5 kHz. The switching loss is 3 mJ × 5000 = 15 W. The total is about 55 W. Through 0.4 °C per watt, the junction rises about 22 °C. With air at 40 °C, it runs near 62 °C. Held half on instead, it would make 400² ÷ (4 × 10) = 4000 W.

**Common mistakes**
- Thinking half on is a safe middle. With a resistive load, it is the hottest setting.
- Thinking the full voltage across an off switch heats it. With almost no current, it makes almost no heat.
- Thinking nearly on is good enough. At 90% on, the switch on 600 V and 30 Ω makes 1080 W.
- Thinking a different device cures half on. The circuit sets the voltage and the current.
- Forgetting the edges. Switching loss climbs with frequency.
- Switching a coil with no freewheeling diode. The spike can break the switch down.

applied: explain.text: "Kept fully on or fully off" and "more heat than it can shed" are stated of every power transistor, but linear regulators and amplifiers run them half on by design; the current is not "forced to stop" (the switch tries, then breaks down); a MOSFET gate leaks a little; a reversed freewheeling diode …

practice.text: The freewheeling-diode step does not say which way round: fitted the other way it shorts the supply each time the switch turns on. The rule of thumb is more general than the narrowed explanation, as linear regulators and amplifiers run power transistors half on.

interactive.whatAmILookingAt: Screen 7 says a MOSFET gate draws current "only" while changing over (it leaks a tiny amount); screens 11 and 12 say the coil current "is forced" to zero in 0.5 µs, but with no diode the switch only tries to, and breaks down as its voltage soars.
notes: explain.text: "Both give the load about 300 V on average" is true, but into a resistor half-time chopping delivers about twice the power of half on (about 6 kW against 3 kW). At equal load power, about 25% on, switching still makes only about 30 W at 10 kHz, so the point stands; the frozen 75-times figure rests …

sources[1]: The 0.7 V freewheeling drop is the sourced small-signal silicon value; a power diode carrying about 20 A usually drops nearer 1 to 1.5 V. It only moves the 601 V figure by a volt or so, and the course uses 0.7 V throughout.
